blindSummary:
This state/province is one of twelve operating a parallel religious criminal-code system - its religious penal code took effect 26 December 2000 - and one of five belt states where religious-morality police activity is specifically documented in a foreign government's 2019 implementation study. Religious courts here have criminal jurisdiction for adherents of the state religion, criminalising conduct beyond the federal statute, including same-sex acts between women (discretionary penalties). No trans-specific incident or carried-out capital sentence is on record for this unit.

The combination of enacted religious criminal jurisdiction and documented morality-police infrastructure is the unit's distinguishing profile within the belt; the belt's cascade began in another state, and morality-police documentation plus case-level studies concentrate in a subset including this unit.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's report section on the extension of religious criminal law: one belt state's governor triggered the cascade (establishment law of 27 October 1999, in force from 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve states - the belt - operate religious criminal jurisdiction. It applies only to adherents of the state religion; others are tried in parallel common-law courts, and the state attorney general oversees both systems.

NOTE: document not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying 2019 implementation study by a foreign government's religious-freedom commission samples 173 religious-court cases (2017) in three belt states and lists this state among the five with documented religious-morality police activity.

Another government's country-of-origin information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression in this country (June 2025): the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct (up to 14 years, attempted acts 3 years) and is silent on women; religious penal codes in the twelve belt states apply only to adherents of the state religion, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death (in a minority of states) to flogging and imprisonment; its enforcement section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and notes few secular cases reach court.
